own_scenes.desc: El sello de Tony Wilson, presentador de televisión educado en Cambridge y admirador de los situacionistas. Peter Saville le da una identidad visual de austeridad modernista (Bauhaus, De Stijl, constructivismo); el catálogo numera cualquier cosa (FAC 8, un temporizador menstrual de Linder; FAC 99, la factura del dentista de Rob Gretton). Sin contratos, «continua negación a la ganancia» y una firme voluntad federalista frente a Londres.

notes.chapter: Cap. 7: Solo hazte a un lado: The Fall, Joy Division y la escena de Manchester
notes.text: Con la muerte de Curtis, Factory queda condenado a buscar otra Joy Division. A Certain Ratio, funk noir influido por The Pop Group (shorts caqui, la batería de Donald Johnson, «Flight»); The Durutti Column, la guitarra de escarcha y Echoplex de Vini Reilly («Missing Boy»); clones como Section 25 y Crispy Ambulance, todos con el sonido de Hannett, que también produce a John Cooper Clarke con The Invisible Girls.

notes.chapter: Cap. 16: Mutant disco y punk funk: tráfico urbano en Nueva York a principios de los ochenta (y más allá)
notes.text: A Certain Ratio graba To Each... en Nueva York con Hannett, que le quita el funk; se enamoran de la ciudad, de sus congas en Central Park, y casi graban un disco con Grace Jones.

refs.q: Reclutó al joven estudiante de diseño Peter Saville para que le diera a Factory su propia identidad visual
refs.para: "Muchísimo más arty que nosotros. Si hubiera podido poner cáscara de naranja en una bolsa de plástico y lanzarla al mercado con un número de catálogo, ¡habría estado muy orgulloso de mí mismo!". Anfitrión y presentador de programas en la televisión local, Wilson era un esteta/agitador educado en Cambridge que amaba el packaging de los discos y quería que su sello tuviera una estética de diseño clara. Reclutó al joven estudiante de diseño Peter Saville para que le diera a Factory su propia identidad visual, influenciada por la austeridad y el severo funcionalismo de los movimientos de diseño moder- nistas de principios del siglo XX como la Bauhaus, De Stijl, el constructivismo y Die Neue Typographie. La tipografía del sello y las tapas de los discos creadas por Saville hacían que Factory y sus bandas -Joy Division, Durutti Column, A Certain Ratio- se separaran del montón postpunk. La elegancia austera era algo nuevo en el packaging del rock, un corte purificador tanto respecto del romanticismo prepunk como de los propios clichés de la new wave. El primer lanzamiento del sello, A Factory Sample, era un EP doble enfundado en plateado brillante. "Se veía tan especial", dice Paul Morley, que por aquel entonces era corresponsal de New Musical Express en Manchester.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Autonomía en el Reino Unido: do it yourself y el movimiento de los sellos independientes británicos

refs.q: Wilson estaba decidido a resistirse a la atracción centrípeta de Londres
refs.para: Esta cuestión de la independencia versus la infiltración, el regionalismo versus la centralización, era un área en la que Fase Produce y Factory disentían enfáticamente. Tony Wilson había visto cómo los primeros sellos indie de Manchester, New Hormones y Rabid, se habían rendido ante el capital. Wilson recuerda preguntarle a Tosh Ryan, de Rabid, en el otoño de 1 977, por qué había dejado que las compañías discográficas de Londres se llevaran a sus mejores artistas, Jilced John y John Cooper Clarke. "Todavía puedo verlo -diciendo: 'Ah, ser independientes solo fue un pequeño período de idealismo que atravesamos'. Era como si la única razón de ser de los sellos indie fuese existir por unos pocos meses, solo por el tiempo necesario para que los managers pudieran conseguirles a sus bandas contratos con discográficas importantes." Wilson estaba decidido a resistirse a la atracción centrípeta de Londres y a construir una base de poder en Manchester, la ciudad que amaba. Su ferviente declaración de principios federalista y pro-ciudades de provincias fue imitada por otros sellos indie en toda Gran Bretaña, especialmente en el Norte y en Escocia. Durante algún tiempo, el chart de álbumes independientes incluyó invariablemente dos o tres compilaciones regionales o de alguna ciudad en particular cada semana, como Is the �r Over? de Cardiff y Bouquet of Steel de Sheffield.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Autonomía en el Reino Unido: do it yourself y el movimiento de los sellos independientes británicos

refs.q: A Certain Ratio y The Durutti Column
refs.para: Mark E. Smith una vez sugirió que había dos clases de fábricas en Manchester: aquellas que producían hombres muertos y aquellas que vivían de un hombre muerto. Un insulto injusto, en verdad en el sentido de que la muerte de Ian Curtis aseguró de una vez y para siempre la futura talla de Factory Records. También condenó al sello a padecer por años la intensa búsqueda de otra banda que tuviera el potencial de ser tan relevante y tan históricamente determinante como Joy Division. De entre las primeras bandas que inflaban las filas de la nómina de Factory, las dos que más cerca estuvieron de ocupar ese lugar fueron A Certain Ratio y The Durutti Column.
refs.chapter: Cap. 7: Solo hazte a un lado: The Fall, Joy Division y la escena de Manchester

refs.q: Altamente influenciado por el sonido de The Pop Group
refs.para: Altamente influenciado por el sonido de The Pop Group (a quienes habían visto en vivo como soporte de Pere Ubu en 1 978), el funk noir de A Certain Ratio se consolidó enormemente cuando reclutaron a un baterista tan bueno como Bruce Smith. Las baterías funk de Donald Johnson evitaban casi por sí solas que el sonido nebuloso de la banda se precipitase irremediablemente hacia el vacío. En "Flight", uno de sus primeros singles, se puede escuchar mejor que en ninguna otra parte la manera en la que la música de A Cenain Ratio trabajaba justo en la tensión entre un funk seco (golpes simultáneos al aro y al parche y redoblantes repiqueteantes, líneas de bajo neuróticas, guitarras rítmicas entrecortadas y nerviosas) e interferencias frías y húmedas, como si proviniesen del interior de una caverna (trompetas que parecían flotar a través de la niebla, manchones difusos de una guitarra tan llena de efectos que, más que una guitarra, parecía un sintetizador}. A veces, A Certain Ratio sonaba como Joy Division poniéndose manos a la obra. El cantante Simon Topping básicamente clonaba el zumbido barítono y monótono de Cunis, y las letras dejaban entrever impulsos oscuros y estados de conciencia sombríos. "A Cenain Ratio tenía un sentido de la moda bizarro; el pelo súper cono, shorts extragrandes color caqui", recuerda Dave Haslam, historiador de la cultura pop de Manchester. Este look, que recordaba vagamente al colonialismo o a las fuerzas militareS alemanas Afrika Korps, se prestaba a ser fácilmente malinterpretado como un coqueteo con el fascismo.

tracks.title: The Return of the Durutti Column

podcast.title: Early Stages and Learning Curve (1978-1979)
podcast.body: At its inception, Factory Records was in its learning phase, with Tony Wilson still figuring out how to run a record label. This period was characterized by a collaborative atmosphere where the label, the band, and the producer were all learning and defining their roles simultaneously. "Toni Wilson acaba de estener su disco gráfica, no sabía muy bien cómo hacerlo"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk

podcast.title: Formation (1978)
podcast.body: Factory Records was one of three important independent labels, alongside Rough Trade and Mute Records, that began releasing material in 1978. These labels emerged with non-commercial aims after the punk revolution opened doors for riskier music. "actor y records... empezaron a literar material en ese mismo año 1978."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: The Haçienda Management and Serial Numbers (1982-1997)
podcast.body: Factory Records, headed by Tony Wilson, was the label behind New Order and the concept originator for The Haçienda nightclub. Like all its projects, the club was given a serial number, FAC51, underscoring its integrated role within the label's artistic and business ventures. "Anyway, like all factory projects and record releases, it had a serial number. FAC51, FAC51."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Aesthetic Focus and Hacienda Nightclub
podcast.body: The label was known for its strong aesthetic, meticulous attention to album artwork and packaging, and a quirky cataloging system. It also established the Hacienda nightclub, which became a central hub for British dance culture throughout the 1980s. "And with Factory, it was more than just about the music. It was all about the aesthetic, the care given to album artwork and packaging, the quirkiness of their cataloging system, the establishment of the Hasey end nightclub, which became ground zero for so much of British dance culture throughout the 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Artistic Freedom Policy
podcast.body: Factory Records was known for allowing its artists, such as the Happy Mondays, considerable artistic freedom, letting them "do what we want" despite having formal contracts. "They would pray. They would let us do what we want."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of "Madchester" - Part 2

podcast.title: Bankruptcy Cause
podcast.body: Factory Records' bankruptcy was primarily due to bad management, not excessive spending by bands like the Happy Mondays, who were actually owed significant money by the label when it went under. "Bad management broke them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Bankruptcy Cause
podcast.body: Factory Records' eventual disbandment and financial collapse are attributed to "bad management," not solely to the Happy Mondays' excessive spending as widely believed. The label still owed the Happy Mondays a substantial amount of money when it went under. "Bad management broke them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of "Madchester" - Part 2

podcast.title: Bankrupted by Happy Mondays
podcast.body: The drug habits of the band Happy Mondays were so extreme that they ultimately led to the financial collapse and demise of their record label, Factory Records. "Their drug habits killed their record label factory records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: RockNRoll Drugs

podcast.title: Business Acumen and Bankruptcy
podcast.body: Factory Records was notably inept at business. A prime example is "Blue Monday," where substantial investment in the sleeve's design and printing resulted in a loss of 30 pence per copy sold, totaling "tens of thousands of pounds." This mismanagement ultimately led to Factory going bankrupt twice. "This highlights a problem with many of those great British indie labels of the 80s. They were crap at doing business. Factory would eventually go bankrupt twice..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 9

podcast.title: Business Challenges and Bankruptcy
podcast.body: Despite its musical influence, Factory Records faced significant business challenges, including never asking bands to sign formal contracts, dubious accounting practices, and a consistent lack of attention to cash flow. As a result, the label eventually went spectacularly bankrupt. "As a business, Factory was a basket case, and eventually they went broke in a spectacular way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Co-owner of The Hacienda
podcast.body: Factory Records co-owned The Hacienda, a famous club in Manchester, along with New Order. The club was initially financially troubled but became a vibrant center of UK club culture, known for its pivotal role in the rave scene, before its eventual decline. "the infamous club owned by New Order and Factory Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 10

podcast.title: Coined "Postmodern" Music
podcast.body: Label boss Tony Wilson, characterized as an "intellectual art snob," coined the term "postmodern" to describe the music he was promoting, specifically applying it to groups such as Joy Division. His intention was to integrate the aesthetic principles of actual postmodernism from the art world into the categorization of this new music. "He chose that term because it seemed to fulfill his need to apply the aesthetic of actual postmodernism in the art world to this music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

podcast.title: First Release
podcast.body: Factory Records' inaugural release occurred on December 24, 1978. It consisted of two 7-inch singles bundled together, featuring samples from four bands on its roster, with Side A including two songs by Joy Division, notably "Digital." "The very first factory release was issued on December 24, 1978. Two 7-inch singles bundled together featuring samples from four bands in the roster."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Foundation and Launch with Joy Division
podcast.body: Founded by music critic Tony Wilson, Factory Records was a new label that had not yet represented any artists when Joy Division contacted Wilson. Joy Division's signing and subsequent work effectively launched Factory Records, making their output the label's first relevant release. "había fundado su primera discográfica que era factor y records, pero efectos prácticos es como si factor y records no se hiciera. Estaba la acabada arrancar, no estaba representando a nadie."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk

podcast.title: Founded by Tony Wilson
podcast.body: This label was founded by Manchester TV host Tony Wilson, who was inspired after attending the Sex Pistols show in 1976. The name "Factory Records" was derived from a local nightclub night. "He called the company Factory Records after a local nightclub night."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Founding After Sex Pistols' Impact
podcast.body: Tony Wilson established Factory Records following the highly influential Sex Pistols performance at Manchester's Lesser Free Trade Hall in the mid-1970s. The label subsequently became home to seminal bands like Joy Division and many others who shaped the post-punk and Madchester scenes. "Tony Wilson found factory records and then we get, you know, joy division and everything that comes after that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of "Madchester" - Part 1

podcast.title: Founding and Early Success
podcast.body: Tony Wilson founded Factory Records, which quickly began to achieve significant success. "Tony Wilson acababa de hacer fondar su disco gráfica factor el récords con las que empezaba a tener un exito importante."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 4. La banda tras el final

podcast.title: Founding and Influence in Manchester
podcast.body: Factory Records was founded by Tony Wilson, who also discovered Joy Division and Happy Mondays. As a record label, it generated significant income and played a crucial role in the development and spread of the Manchester movement. "Tony Wilson, si el mismo Tony Wilson que había fundado Factory Records y que había descubierto a Joey Division es el padre absoluto del movimiento Manchester. El era original de Manchester, crítico musical, funda a Factory Records la discográfica con la que descubra Joey Division y que gana muchísimo dinero pero también con la que descubriría los capi-mondes y una parte importante de este movimiento Manchester"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Sonido MADCHESTER

podcast.title: Founding and Mission
podcast.body: Factory Records was a prominent British indie label established by Tony Wilson, a TV host from Manchester, who sought to showcase the music of his city. Its history is "lightly fictionalized" in the movie "24 Hour Party People." "Factory, which was founded by Tony Wilson, a TV host and manchester who decided that someone needed to showcase the music of his city."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 9

podcast.title: Founding with Inheritance
podcast.body: Tony Wilson, a TV personality, started Factory Records using a modest inheritance he received after a relative died. In January 1979, the label issued its first record, "Factory Sampler," featuring material from new bands, including Joy Division. "Soon after that battle, the band showed one of Tony Wilson's relatives die, leaving him a modest inheritance. And what did he do with that money? He started a record company called Factory."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Funding 'Unknown Pleasures'
podcast.body: Tony Wilson was so impressed with the recording of Joy Division's "Unknown Pleasures" that he invested all of Factory Records' money, 8,500 pounds, to press up 10,000 copies of the album. "Tony Wilson, they had a factory, was so thrilled with the results that he put up 8,500 pounds, all the money factory had to press up 10,000 copies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Happy Mondays Association
podcast.body: Factory Records was the label for Happy Mondays, one of the "Holy Trinity" bands of the Madchester scene in the late 1980s and early 1990s. "the Happy Mondays, part of factory records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Indie Rock: Part 4

podcast.title: Importance to The Durutti Column
podcast.body: Factory Records considered The Durutti Column, a band that Dave Rowbotham was a part of, to be "very important." This highlights the label's recognition of the band's significance within the punk and post-punk scenes. "He was in a bunch of punk and post-punk bands before landing in the Deritty column, a group considered to be very important by factory records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Stars Who Were Murdered

podcast.title: In-House Art Director Peter Saville
podcast.body: Peter Saville served as Factory Records' in-house art director, responsible for creating the iconic black cover design for Joy Division's "Unknown Pleasures" album, featuring the ridge line plot of a pulsar. "One of the most striking features of the album was the cover design by Factory Records in-house art director Peter Savile."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Independent Label in Post-Punk Era
podcast.body: Factory Records was one of the many independent labels that emerged in the wake of punk, providing a platform for artists like Joy Division. "They recorded four factory records, one of the many independent labels that sprung up in the wake of punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7

podcast.title: Independent Manchester Label
podcast.body: Factory Records was an independent record label established in Manchester by Tony Wilson. It played a pivotal role in championing the nascent sounds emanating from the city, most notably signing and supporting groups like Joy Division. "That along came Tony Wilson. Factory records his new independent record label based up Manchester, championed some of the new sounds coming out of the city and being something of an entrepreneur he needed to find a brand name for the kind of music he was pushing if he was ever going to sell it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

podcast.title: Influential Art Design (1970s-1980s)
podcast.body: Factory Records, based in Manchester, was a renowned company where Peter Saville served as the chief art design guy. Saville was responsible for a wide range of design work, including gig posters and album covers for prominent bands such as Joy Division, New Order, Roxy Music, Suede, Pulp, Martha and the Muffins, and No Means No. "Seville was the chief art design guy at factory records back in the day, the famous company based on a Manchester. He did everything from gig posters to album design for Joy Division New Order, Roxas music, Swade, pulp, Martha Nemuffins, and Noam D."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 2: Album Artwork

podcast.title: Influential British Indie Label
podcast.body: Factory Records is recognized as one of the great British indie labels of all time, serving as the source for influential music from bands such as Joy Division, New Order, Happy Mondays, and Cabaret Voltaire. "Factory went on to become one of the great British indie labels of all time. So much music flowed from this company."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Influential British Indie Label
podcast.body: Factory Records is recognized as an influential British indie label, mentioned alongside Creation and Sarah Records. It played a significant role in establishing a distinct identity for the British indie sound and style, particularly in the context and spirit of the C86 movement. "Like factory records, creation, and a few others, Sarah Records helped bring an identity to the British indie sound and style, exemplified by the whole C86 movement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Twee Pop: A History

podcast.title: Manchester-Based Independent Label
podcast.body: Factory Records was an independent label based out of Manchester, which was not considered a "cool place to be" at the time compared to London. It was the label for archetypical British indie band Joy Division. "They recorded it for factory, an independent label based out of Manchester when Manchester really wasn't much of a cool place to be for anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Out of Business
podcast.body: Factory Records eventually went out of business, contributing to the decline of the Madchester scene, alongside other issues faced by its prominent bands and venues. "and factory records was out of business. Again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Part of Manchester Indie Scene
podcast.body: Factory Records was a significant label within the Manchester scene, which played a big part in the deep entrenchment of indie culture across the UK by the 1990s. "The Manchester scene was a big part of that thanks to labels like Factory."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Snob

podcast.title: Protagonist in Manchester Movement
podcast.body: Factory Records was a key protagonist in the Manchester movement, which Tony Wilson, through the label and The Haçienda, nearly invented. "Y nací oficialmente el pistoletazo de salida al movimiento Manchester del que Toni Wilson, mi factor y records eran protagonistas absolutos, el descubrió a los Habimondas y el descubrió casi el casi inventó el movimiento Manchester entre el efecto y el récord y la cienda."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 4. La banda tras el final

podcast.title: Relationship with Happy Mondays
podcast.body: Factory Records had a complex relationship with the Happy Mondays; while head Tony Wilson loved the band, many others at the label, including other bands and managers, did not take to them. "Everyone at Factory hated us, apart from Tony loved us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Rob Gretton's Influence
podcast.body: Factory Records was a new, "very cool" indie label. Rob Gretton, manager of Joy Division, played a key role in its growth by helping to sign other significant acts like Happy Mondays and OMD to the label.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock

podcast.title: The Haçienda Co-ownership
podcast.body: Factory Records co-owned The Haçienda, the Manchester nightclub that was a central part of the acid house rave scene. "the Haseyenda, the Manchester Nightclub co-owned by New Order in factory records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Tony Wilson's Character
podcast.body: Tony Wilson, the head of Factory Records, was described as more of an artist and a supporter of artists than a shrewd businessman. "Tony wasn't the greatest businessman. He was, he was an artist and a supporter of the artist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of Manchester Part 2

podcast.title: Tony Wilson's Role
podcast.body: Tony Wilson, associated with Factory Records, was a proponent of the theory that rock and pop music are engaged in a death struggle, playing out in cycles. His involvement lends credibility to historical observations about the cyclical nature of music trends. "That theory contends that rock and pop music are locked in a death struggle that plays itself out like clockwork every 13 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Tony Wilson's Role
podcast.body: Tony Wilson, the founder, was described as a "great guy" and primarily "an artist and a supporter of the artist," rather than a shrewd businessman. He was particularly supportive of the Happy Mondays, even when others at the label or other bands disliked them. "Tony wasn't the greatest businessman. He was an artist and a supporter of the artist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Oral History of "Madchester" - Part 2
